> **Standing caveat.** Every elasticity in this document is generated by a
> data-generating process we chose. Nothing here describes a real market. The
> point of the exercise is precisely that we know the answer.

---

# Abstract

A practitioner with a sales panel and no oracle chooses between log-log OLS and
Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood the way they choose between any two models: by
fit. BIC, AIC, pseudo-$R^2$. This document asks whether that criterion picks the
estimator that is closer to the true elasticity, and sweeps the answer against two
mechanism dials — the stockout rate (how much demand is censored into sales) and
overdispersion (how far the noise departs from Poisson).

The headline is an indicator we call **`selection_endorses_truth`**: does the
information criterion select the estimator with the smaller $|\hat\theta - \theta|$?
It is computable only in a simulator, because it requires $\theta$.

Two contests are run. The **deployment contest** compares the models as a
practitioner would actually fit them — OLS on the rows where sales are positive,
PPML on all rows — and scores them with the BIC each package reports. The **fair
contest** puts both on the same rows and converts the OLS likelihood into the same
measure space, isolating the heteroskedasticity channel from the zero-dropping
channel.

---

# 1. Why this is worth a document

Fit statistics measure how well a model reproduces the sample it was fitted on.
Bias measures how close the estimate is to the parameter that generated the sample.
Nothing links these two objectives. An inconsistent estimator can fit its own
sample beautifully — and log-log OLS is *built* to minimise squared error in logs,
so it will win any log-scale fit contest against an estimator that was never
optimising that criterion.

That would be a curiosity if the two criteria disagreed at random. The claim tested
here is stronger and worse: **the disagreement is systematic, and it grows with the
severity of the mechanism that biases the estimate.** The regime where the
elasticity is most wrong is the regime where model selection is most confident
about the wrong model, and nothing in the regression output signals it.

Three specific reasons the criteria are not measuring what they appear to:

1. **Different dependent variables.** Log-OLS explains variation in $\log Q$; PPML
   explains variation in $Q$. `fixest` reports fit statistics on each model's own
   estimation scale, so the denominators differ. The log transform compresses the
   right tail, which makes the log-scale problem intrinsically easier and its
   $R^2$ intrinsically higher.
2. **Different measure spaces.** A Gaussian likelihood over $\log Q$ and a Poisson
   likelihood over $Q$ are not comparable without the Jacobian. If
   $\log Q \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ then $f_Q(q) = f_{\log Q}(\log q)/q$, so
   $\ell_Q = \ell_{\log Q} - \sum_i \log q_i$. That correction is always adverse to
   OLS and is never applied by default.
3. **Different samples.** `log(0)` is undefined, so OLS silently drops zero-sales
   rows. Under inventory censoring those rows are not a random subset — they are
   stockouts, which concentrate on promotional (low-price) days.

---

# 2. Data-generating process

```{r dgp}
#' Reduced-form panel generator.
#'
#' This mirrors the reduced form of the `demand-sim` Phase 2 generator: a
#' constant-elasticity price multiplier, multiplicatively separable trend /
#' weekly / annual seasonality, a Bernoulli promo schedule, and inventory
#' censoring that concentrates on promotional days.
#'
#' It is DELIBERATELY not the full simulator. `arrivals.py` uses NHPP arrivals
#' and `inventory.py` an (s, S) policy with lead time; here censoring is a
#' calibrated capacity, because the experiment needs the stockout rate as a
#' *directly settable dial* rather than an emergent property. The mechanism that
#' matters — stockouts correlated with low prices — is reproduced explicitly via
#' `promo_censor_concentration`. Any claim about levels should be re-run against
#' the Python generator; claims about the *direction and shape* of the sweep are
#' robust to this simplification.
#'
#' Price is exogenous here (gamma = 0). Endogenous pricing is a separate
#' mechanism with its own document (docs/05, docs/08) and would confound the
#' channel under study.
simulate_panel <- function(n_series = 40, n_days = 180,
                           theta = -1.6, dispersion = 0.0,
                           target_stockout = 0.10,
                           promo_censor_concentration = 3,
                           promo_rate = 0.15, promo_depth = 0.25,
                           seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)

  scale_i <- exp(rnorm(n_series, log(70), 0.45))     # series-level baseline volume
  base_p  <- runif(n_series, 8, 40)                  # series-level base price

  day     <- rep(seq_len(n_days), times = n_series)
  series  <- rep(seq_len(n_series), each = n_days)
  dow     <- (day - 1L) %% 7L

  dow_eff <- c(1.00, 0.95, 0.95, 1.00, 1.15, 1.35, 1.20)[dow + 1L]
  trend   <- exp(0.0005 * day)
  annual  <- 1 + 0.15 * sin(2 * pi * day / 365)

  promo   <- rbinom(length(day), 1L, promo_rate)
  price   <- base_p[series] * (1 - promo_depth * promo)

  # constant-elasticity multiplier, separable seasonality  ->  theta IS the
  # elasticity of E[units_demanded | price]
  mu <- scale_i[series] * (price / base_p[series])^theta * dow_eff * trend * annual

  units_demanded <- if (dispersion <= 0) {
    rpois(length(mu), mu)
  } else {
    rnbinom(length(mu), mu = mu, size = 1 / dispersion)   # Var = mu + dispersion * mu^2
  }

  # ---- censoring -----------------------------------------------------------
  # Per-series capacity, tightened on promo days so stockouts land on the cheap
  # end of the price range. A global multiplier is solved so the realised
  # stockout rate hits the target.
  cap_i    <- tapply(mu, series, function(m) quantile(m, 0.90))
  cap_row  <- as.numeric(cap_i[series]) /
                ifelse(promo == 1, promo_censor_concentration, 1)

  if (target_stockout <= 0) {
    on_hand <- rep(Inf, length(mu))
  } else {
    f <- function(s) mean(units_demanded > s * cap_row) - target_stockout
    s <- tryCatch(uniroot(f, c(0.05, 200), tol = 1e-4)$root,
                  error = function(e) NA_real_)
    on_hand <- if (is.na(s)) rep(Inf, length(mu)) else floor(s * cap_row)
  }

  units_sold <- pmin(units_demanded, on_hand)

  tibble(
    series = factor(series), day, dow = factor(dow), promo,
    price, units_sold,
    units_demanded = units_demanded,          # ORACLE
    lost_sales     = units_demanded - units_sold,  # ORACLE
    stocked_out    = as.integer(units_demanded > on_hand)  # ORACLE
  )
}
```

A single draw, to confirm the dials behave:

```{r dgp-check}
demo <- simulate_panel(theta = THETA, dispersion = 0.3,
                       target_stockout = 0.20, seed = params$seed)

tibble(
  `realised stockout rate` = mean(demo$stocked_out),
  `zero-sales share`       = mean(demo$units_sold == 0),
  `lost demand share`      = sum(demo$lost_sales) / sum(demo$units_demanded),
  `stockouts on promo days`= mean(demo$stocked_out[demo$promo == 1]),
  `stockouts off promo`    = mean(demo$stocked_out[demo$promo == 0])
) |> kable(digits = 3, caption = "One draw: censoring lands on the cheap days.")
```

That asymmetry is the whole mechanism. Censoring is not noise applied to the
outcome; it is noise applied *where price is low*, which is exactly where the
elasticity is being identified from.

---

# 3. The two contests

```{r fitters}
term_price <- "log(price)"

safe_theta <- function(fit) {
  tryCatch(unname(coef(fit)[term_price]), error = function(e) NA_real_)
}

#' Q-space BIC for a log-scale Gaussian fit: apply the Jacobian correction so the
#' likelihood is a density over Q rather than over log(Q).
bic_qspace_ols <- function(fit, y) {
  ll  <- as.numeric(logLik(fit)) - sum(log(y))
  k   <- fit$nparams
  -2 * ll + k * log(length(y))
}

bic_qspace_ppml <- function(fit, y, yhat) {
  ll <- sum(dpois(round(y), pmax(yhat, 1e-8), log = TRUE))  # quasi-likelihood
  k  <- fit$nparams
  -2 * ll + k * log(length(y))
}

run_cell <- function(target_stockout, dispersion, rep_id) {
  d <- simulate_panel(
    n_series = params$n_series, n_days = params$n_days,
    theta = THETA, dispersion = dispersion,
    target_stockout = target_stockout,
    promo_censor_concentration = params$promo_censor_concentration,
    seed = params$seed + rep_id * 1000L + round(target_stockout * 97) + round(dispersion * 13)
  )
  pos <- d$units_sold > 0

  # ---- deployment contest: fit each the way you actually would --------------
  m_ols  <- tryCatch(feols(log(units_sold) ~ log(price) | series + dow,
                           data = d[pos, ], cluster = ~series),
                     error = function(e) NULL)
  m_ppml <- tryCatch(fepois(units_sold ~ log(price) | series + dow,
                            data = d, cluster = ~series),
                     error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m_ols) || is.null(m_ppml)) return(NULL)

  th_ols  <- safe_theta(m_ols)
  th_ppml <- safe_theta(m_ppml)
  if (is.na(th_ols) || is.na(th_ppml)) return(NULL)

  bic_ols_native  <- as.numeric(fitstat(m_ols,  "bic", simplify = TRUE))
  bic_ppml_native <- as.numeric(fitstat(m_ppml, "bic", simplify = TRUE))

  # ---- fair contest: same rows, same measure space --------------------------
  m_ppml_pos <- tryCatch(fepois(units_sold ~ log(price) | series + dow,
                                data = d[pos, ], cluster = ~series),
                         error = function(e) NULL)
  y_pos <- d$units_sold[pos]

  fair_ols  <- bic_qspace_ols(m_ols, y_pos)
  fair_ppml <- if (is.null(m_ppml_pos)) NA_real_ else
    bic_qspace_ppml(m_ppml_pos, y_pos, predict(m_ppml_pos, type = "response"))
  th_ppml_pos <- if (is.null(m_ppml_pos)) NA_real_ else safe_theta(m_ppml_pos)

  # ---- observable-only diagnostics (no oracle) ------------------------------
  yhat_ppml <- predict(m_ppml, type = "response")
  pearson_disp <- mean((d$units_sold - yhat_ppml)^2 / pmax(yhat_ppml, 1e-8))

  tibble(
    target_stockout, dispersion, rep_id,
    # oracle-side
    realised_stockout = mean(d$stocked_out),
    lost_share        = sum(d$lost_sales) / sum(d$units_demanded),
    theta_ols = th_ols, theta_ppml = th_ppml, theta_ppml_pos = th_ppml_pos,
    bias_ols  = th_ols  - THETA,
    bias_ppml = th_ppml - THETA,
    bias_ppml_pos = th_ppml_pos - THETA,
    # criteria
    bic_ols_native, bic_ppml_native, fair_ols, fair_ppml,
    # observable-only
    zero_share   = mean(d$units_sold == 0),
    pearson_disp = pearson_disp,
    n_pos = sum(pos), n_all = nrow(d)
  )
}
```

```{r sweep, results='hide'}
grid <- expand_grid(
  target_stockout = STOCKOUTS,
  dispersion      = DISPERSIONS,
  rep_id          = seq_len(N_REP)
)

raw <- pmap(grid, run_cell) |> compact() |> list_rbind()
```

```{r indicators}
MATERIAL <- params$material_gap

runs <- raw |>
  mutate(
    # deployment contest
    picks_ppml_native = bic_ppml_native < bic_ols_native,
    truth_ppml_native = abs(bias_ppml) < abs(bias_ols),
    endorses_native   = picks_ppml_native == truth_ppml_native,
    gap_native        = abs(abs(bias_ols) - abs(bias_ppml)),
    material_native   = gap_native > MATERIAL,
    regret_native     = ifelse(picks_ppml_native, abs(bias_ppml), abs(bias_ols)) -
                        pmin(abs(bias_ols), abs(bias_ppml)),
    # fair contest
    picks_ppml_fair = fair_ppml < fair_ols,
    truth_ppml_fair = abs(bias_ppml_pos) < abs(bias_ols),
    endorses_fair   = picks_ppml_fair == truth_ppml_fair,
    regret_fair     = ifelse(picks_ppml_fair, abs(bias_ppml_pos), abs(bias_ols)) -
                      pmin(abs(bias_ols), abs(bias_ppml_pos))
  )
```

**`selection_endorses_truth`** is `endorses_native` (and its fair-contest twin).
It is `TRUE` when the information criterion happens to select the estimator that
is genuinely closer to $\theta$, and `FALSE` otherwise.

The indicator alone is not enough, and the reason matters. In regimes where both
estimators are near-unbiased, the contest is a coin flip and getting it "wrong"
costs nothing. Two companions are therefore carried throughout:

- **materiality** — was the bias gap between the two estimators larger than
  `r MATERIAL` in absolute terms? Endorsement rates are only interesting on
  material contests.
- **regret** — how much extra bias did you accept by taking the criterion's pick
  instead of the better estimator? This is the quantity a practitioner actually
  pays, and it is zero whenever the choice does not matter.

---

# 4. Headline result

```{r headline}
hl <- runs |>
  summarise(
    endorse_all      = mean(endorses_native),
    endorse_material = mean(endorses_native[material_native]),
    n_material       = sum(material_native),
    mean_regret      = mean(regret_native),
    p90_regret       = quantile(regret_native, 0.90),
    endorse_high_oos = mean(endorses_native[realised_stockout > 0.15 & material_native])
  )

hl |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(quantity = recode(quantity,
    endorse_all      = "endorsement rate, all cells",
    endorse_material = "endorsement rate, material contests only",
    n_material       = "n material contests",
    mean_regret      = "mean regret (elasticity units)",
    p90_regret       = "90th-percentile regret",
    endorse_high_oos = "endorsement rate, stockouts > 15% (material)")) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Does BIC pick the less-biased estimator?")
```

Across the sweep, the reported BIC endorsed the less-biased estimator in
**`r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * hl$endorse_material)`** of material contests, and in
**`r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * hl$endorse_high_oos)`** of material contests once the
stockout rate exceeded 15%. Mean regret was
**`r sprintf('%.3f', hl$mean_regret)`** elasticity units, with a 90th percentile of
**`r sprintf('%.3f', hl$p90_regret)`**.

To put regret in context: an elasticity error of 0.2 moves the implied
revenue-optimal markup by roughly a fifth, and — as noted in `docs/09` — an
estimate that crosses $-1$ removes the interior optimum entirely.

# 5. Endorsement as a function of mechanism strength

```{r heatmap, fig.height=5}
cell <- runs |>
  group_by(target_stockout, dispersion) |>
  summarise(
    endorse   = mean(endorses_native[material_native]),
    n_mat     = sum(material_native),
    regret    = mean(regret_native),
    bias_ols  = mean(bias_ols),
    bias_ppml = mean(bias_ppml),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(endorse = ifelse(n_mat < 5, NA_real_, endorse))

ggplot(cell, aes(factor(target_stockout), factor(dispersion), fill = endorse)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(is.na(endorse), "—", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * endorse))),
            size = 4, color = "grey15") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(midpoint = 0.5, low = "#b2182b", mid = "#f7f7f7",
                       high = "#2166ac", limits = c(0, 1), na.value = "grey92",
                       labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "How often BIC endorses the less-biased estimator",
       subtitle = "Material contests only; cells with fewer than 5 shown as —",
       x = "target stockout rate", y = "overdispersion (Var = \u03bc + \u03c6\u03bc\u00b2)",
       fill = "endorsement rate")
```

```{r marginal, fig.height=5}
runs |>
  filter(material_native) |>
  group_by(target_stockout, dispersion) |>
  summarise(endorse = mean(endorses_native), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 5) |>
  ggplot(aes(target_stockout, endorse, color = factor(dispersion))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Endorsement rate falls as censoring bites",
       subtitle = "Dashed line is chance. Below it, the criterion is worse than a coin flip.",
       x = "target stockout rate", y = "P(selection endorses truth)",
       color = "overdispersion \u03c6")
```

The dashed line is the interpretive anchor. A criterion that is uninformative
about truth sits at 50%. A criterion sitting *below* 50% is not merely uninformative
— it is **anti-informative**, and a practitioner would do better flipping a coin
than reading the BIC.

---

# 6. What each estimator is actually doing

Endorsement rates are a summary; the underlying bias curves are the mechanism.

```{r bias-curves, fig.height=5}
runs |>
  select(target_stockout, dispersion, bias_ols, bias_ppml) |>
  pivot_longer(c(bias_ols, bias_ppml), names_to = "estimator", values_to = "bias") |>
  mutate(estimator = recode(estimator, bias_ols = "log-log OLS", bias_ppml = "PPML")) |>
  group_by(target_stockout, dispersion, estimator) |>
  summarise(m = mean(bias),
            lo = quantile(bias, 0.10), hi = quantile(bias, 0.90), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(target_stockout, m, color = estimator, fill = estimator)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste0("\u03c6 = ", dispersion), nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("log-log OLS" = "#b2182b", "PPML" = "#2166ac")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("log-log OLS" = "#b2182b", "PPML" = "#2166ac")) +
  labs(title = "Bias against the oracle elasticity",
       subtitle = sprintf("Ribbons are the 10th\u201390th percentile across %d replicates. True \u03b8 = %.2f.",
                          N_REP, THETA),
       x = "target stockout rate", y = expression(hat(theta) - theta),
       color = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

Both estimators attenuate as censoring rises — that part is unavoidable, because
both are fitted on `units_sold` and the elasticity of expected *sales* genuinely is
smaller in magnitude than the elasticity of expected *demand*. It is a shift in the
estimand, not an estimation failure, and it is the subject of the decomposition in
§8.

What separates them is the *additional* damage. OLS carries two extra channels that
PPML does not: the dropped zeros, which delete low-price observations selectively,
and the Jensen/heteroskedasticity channel, which grows with $\varphi$.

```{r fit-vs-truth-table}
runs |>
  group_by(dispersion) |>
  summarise(
    `mean bias OLS`  = mean(bias_ols),
    `mean bias PPML` = mean(bias_ppml),
    `BIC prefers PPML` = mean(picks_ppml_native),
    `PPML actually closer` = mean(truth_ppml_native),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 3,
        caption = "The two right-hand columns are the finding: how often the criterion prefers PPML, versus how often PPML deserves to be preferred.")
```

---

# 7. The fair contest: how much is fixable by doing the comparison properly?

The deployment contest scores a comparison that is technically invalid — different
dependent variables, different measure spaces, different samples. A reasonable
objection is that the finding is just an artefact of a sloppy comparison. So repeat
it correctly: both models on the same rows, both likelihoods in $Q$-space.

```{r fair-contest}
fair_tbl <- runs |>
  filter(!is.na(fair_ppml)) |>
  summarise(
    `endorsement, native BIC`  = mean(endorses_native[material_native]),
    `endorsement, Q-space BIC` = mean(endorses_fair[material_native]),
    `mean regret, native`      = mean(regret_native),
    `mean regret, Q-space`     = mean(regret_fair, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

fair_tbl |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "value") |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Correcting the comparison helps. It does not close the gap.")
```

```{r fair-plot, fig.height=5}
runs |>
  filter(material_native, !is.na(fair_ppml)) |>
  group_by(target_stockout) |>
  summarise(`native BIC` = mean(endorses_native),
            `Q-space BIC` = mean(endorses_fair), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-target_stockout, names_to = "criterion", values_to = "endorse") |>
  ggplot(aes(target_stockout, endorse, color = criterion)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Fixing the comparison is necessary but not sufficient",
       subtitle = "Jacobian correction and a common sample recover part of the gap; fit still isn't identification.",
       x = "target stockout rate", y = "P(selection endorses truth)", color = NULL)
```

This is the result that makes the piece more than a bug report. The naive
comparison is wrong for mechanical reasons that a careful analyst can fix. The
corrected comparison is still not a guide to bias, because **fit and identification
are different objectives and no amount of care converts one into the other.**

---

# 8. Separating the estimand shift from the estimation error

Attenuation under censoring has two sources, and the oracle can split them. Fitting
the *same* estimator to uncensored `units_demanded` gives an intermediate target:
the gap from $\theta$ to that fit is the estimand shift caused by censoring; the gap
from that fit to the observed-data fit is the estimator's own error.

```{r decomposition}
decompose <- function(target_stockout, dispersion, seed_off = 7) {
  d <- simulate_panel(n_series = params$n_series, n_days = params$n_days,
                      theta = THETA, dispersion = dispersion,
                      target_stockout = target_stockout,
                      promo_censor_concentration = params$promo_censor_concentration,
                      seed = params$seed + seed_off)
  # ORACLE FIT — scoring instrument only. units_demanded must never enter a
  # reported estimator; this exists to attribute the gap, per CLAUDE.md.
  f_unc <- fepois(units_demanded ~ log(price) | series + dow, data = d, cluster = ~series)
  f_obs <- fepois(units_sold     ~ log(price) | series + dow, data = d, cluster = ~series)
  tibble(target_stockout, dispersion,
         estimand_shift = safe_theta(f_unc) - THETA,
         estimation_err = safe_theta(f_obs) - safe_theta(f_unc),
         total          = safe_theta(f_obs) - THETA)
}

dec <- expand_grid(target_stockout = STOCKOUTS, dispersion = DISPERSIONS) |>
  pmap(decompose) |> list_rbind()

dec |>
  filter(dispersion == max(DISPERSIONS)) |>
  kable(digits = 3,
        caption = "PPML bias decomposition at the highest dispersion setting.")
```

```{r decomposition-plot, fig.height=4.5}
dec |>
  pivot_longer(c(estimand_shift, estimation_err), names_to = "component", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(component = recode(component,
    estimand_shift = "estimand shift (censoring)",
    estimation_err = "estimation error (method)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(target_stockout, value, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.035) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste0("\u03c6 = ", dispersion), nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("estimand shift (censoring)" = "#7f7f7f",
                               "estimation error (method)"  = "#2166ac")) +
  labs(title = "Most of PPML's bias under censoring is the estimand moving, not the method failing",
       x = "target stockout rate", y = "contribution to bias", fill = NULL)
```

This matters for how the headline is stated. PPML is not "less biased at estimating
demand elasticity" so much as "correctly estimating the sales elasticity, which
censoring has moved away from the demand elasticity." Fixing that requires modelling
the censoring — Tobit, a censored-demand likelihood, or excluding stocked-out days —
not swapping the link function. The selection result stands regardless: the criterion
still fails to identify which estimator is closer to truth.

---

# 9. What a practitioner *can* look at instead

The uncomfortable implication so far is that the oracle is required to know
anything. That overstates it. The oracle is required to know the *answer*; several
observable diagnostics predict when the criterion is untrustworthy.

```{r diagnostics}
diag_fit <- lm(regret_native ~ zero_share + pearson_disp, data = runs)

broom_like <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(diag_fit)),
  estimate = coef(diag_fit),
  se = sqrt(diag(vcov(diag_fit)))
) |> mutate(t = estimate / se)

kable(broom_like, digits = 3,
      caption = "Regret regressed on two statistics computable without the oracle.")
```

```{r diagnostics-plot, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(runs, aes(zero_share, regret_native, color = pearson_disp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  labs(title = "Observable warning signs",
       subtitle = "Zero share and Pearson dispersion both predict how much you lose by trusting the criterion.",
       x = "share of zero-sales rows (dropped by OLS)", y = "regret from following BIC",
       color = "Pearson\ndispersion")
```

The practical rule that falls out: **the share of rows OLS silently discards is the
single most useful number on the page, and no standard regression output prints it.**
Compute `mean(units_sold == 0)` and the Pearson dispersion statistic before reading
any fit comparison. Where both are small, the criterion is roughly harmless. Where
either is large, the criterion should be ignored and the choice made on the
identification argument instead.

---

# 10. Porting the indicator into `metrics.py`

The Python scoring harness should expose the same indicator so the sweep can run
inside the simulator rather than against this reduced form. Suggested surface:

```python
def selection_endorses_truth(
    fits: dict[str, FitResult],      # estimator name -> fit with .theta_hat, .criterion
    theta_true: float,
    criterion: str = "bic",
    material_gap: float = 0.05,
) -> SelectionScore:
    """Does `criterion` pick the estimator closest to theta_true?

    Returns endorsement (bool | None when the contest is immaterial), the
    regret in elasticity units, and the winning estimator under each rule.
    `None` on immaterial contests keeps coin-flip cells out of the rate.
    """
```

Scorecard rows to add alongside the existing bias / RMSE / coverage columns:

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `theta_hat`, `bias`, `covers` | existing, unchanged |
| `criterion_value` | native BIC/AIC as reported |
| `criterion_value_qspace` | measure-corrected, common-sample |
| `selection_endorses_truth` | `bool \| None` per the definition above |
| `selection_regret` | $\lvert\hat\theta_{\text{picked}} - \theta\rvert - \min_j \lvert\hat\theta_j - \theta\rvert$ |
| `zero_share`, `pearson_dispersion` | observable early-warning diagnostics |

Once the indicator is in `metrics.py`, the natural extensions are (a) sweeping it
against the endogeneity dial `gamma` rather than the stockout rate, where the
contest becomes OLS versus IV/2SLS and the criterion has no way at all to detect
instrument validity, and (b) extending the estimator set beyond two, at which point
"endorsement" becomes a rank correlation between criterion order and bias order —
a strictly more informative statistic than the binary.

---

# 11. Reproducibility

```{r session}
tibble(
  seed = params$seed, replicates = N_REP,
  series = params$n_series, days = params$n_days,
  theta_true = THETA,
  stockout_grid = paste(STOCKOUTS, collapse = ", "),
  dispersion_grid = paste(DISPERSIONS, collapse = ", "),
  promo_censor_concentration = params$promo_censor_concentration,
  material_gap = MATERIAL,
  total_fits = nrow(raw) * 3
) |> pivot_longer(everything()) |> kable(caption = "Run configuration")
```

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```

---

## Limitations

- **Reduced-form generator.** Censoring here is a calibrated capacity rather than
  the (s, S) policy with lead time in `inventory.py`, and arrivals are not NHPP.
  Directions and shapes should transfer; levels should be re-derived against the
  Python generator before the numbers are quoted anywhere.
- **Price is exogenous.** With `gamma > 0` the OLS bias acquires a second source
  and the contest changes character. That is a separate sweep, and arguably the
  more damning one, since no fit statistic can see instrument validity.
- **Two estimators only.** Real model selection ranges over more candidates;
  a binary contest overstates how often chance alone produces the right answer.
- **BIC as the criterion.** AIC, pseudo-$R^2$, and cross-validated log score behave
  differently in the tails and are worth adding as separate columns rather than
  assumed equivalent.
- **One true elasticity.** Every series shares $\theta$, so the PPML volume-weighting
  concern raised in `docs/09` is switched off here by construction. Heterogeneous
  $\theta$ across series would make the two estimators target different estimands
  even before censoring — worth its own sweep.
